questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a stock of a resource from a flow of that resource
questions.stem: Ticket ENV-410 asks why the reservoir gauge on our dashboard fell even though the weekly inflow meter read steady all month.

options.text: The stored volume is a stock that can be drawn down, while inflow is only the rate that refills it
The two meters disagree because the inflow sensor counts litres while the gauge reads gallons
options.misconception: treats a unit mismatch as the whole explanation

options.text: A falling gauge always proves the drought was worse than the inflow records captured

questions.explanation: A gauge is a stock measured at an instant; the inflow meter is a flow per unit time. The level falls whenever withdrawals exceed refill, so a falling stock never identifies the flow behind it.
questions.hint: Ask whether the number is a level held or a rate of change.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a renewable source needs balancing
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an intermittent renewable supply needs balancing
questions.stem: The energy platform squad filed a ticket after the wind feed swung from surplus to deficit in one hour.

answer.exemplar: Annual totals hide hourly mismatch. Wind output and demand are not correlated hour by hour, so a surplus year can still contain long low-wind stretches that exceed available supply, and the surplus is not storable at grid scale. Balancing covers the gap with storage, interconnection, dispatchable plant or demand response, sized on the worst net deficit hour rather than on the annual energy balance.

questions.explanation: Annual totals hide the hourly mismatch that causes failure. Surplus in some hours cannot cover deficit in others, so capacity must cover the worst net gap, not the annual balance.
questions.hint: Compare the hourly profile with the annual total.

answer.exemplar: Pair a continuous stage gauge with an inlet flow meter and a withdrawal meter on the same catchment for one hydrological year, and log all three at hourly resolution. questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: The rule that classifies a resource as renewable
questions.learningObjective: Explain the rate-of-renewal test for a resource
questions.stem: Two sprints ago our analytics group documented how a feed source gets labelled.

answer.exemplar: A resource counts as renewable when the rate at which it is regenerated can keep pace with the rate at which it is extracted, and when that regeneration is a natural process rather than a stock being drawn down. A zero-emission test confuses a different property: an unabated fossil source can be used in a way that emits little at the point of use while still depleting a finite stock, and nuclear power emits little while using a fuel that is not renewable.

questions.explanation: Renewability is a rate question about regeneration versus extraction, not an emissions question. A no-emissions test would label several finite fuels renewable and would exclude sources that are renewable but not always clean.
questions.hint: Focus on rate of renewal against rate of use.

questions.topic: Two studies with different boundaries
questions.learningObjective: Test whether two lifecycle studies differ only by boundary
questions.stem: A research-engineering ticket asks how two lifecycle studies of the same asset can disagree.

answer.exemplar: Take the two studies and rebuild each on a single boundary: same functional unit, same assumed lifetime and same allocation rule, then recompute the totals from the original inventory data. Run three variants that add back one excluded stage at a time, for example transport, construction and end-of-life, and record how much of the original gap each stage explains. The result should show whether the remaining difference is a boundary effect or a data and assumption difference.

questions.explanation: Rebuilding both studies on one boundary isolates the boundary effect from differences in data and method. Adding stages back one at a time shows which excluded stage actually explains the gap.
questions.hint: Recompute both on a shared boundary first.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a global hectare assumes about productivity
questions.learningObjective: Explain the productivity assumption inside a global hectare
questions.stem: A docstring task asks us to explain the boundary behind our hectare figure.

answer.exemplar: A global hectare is a productivity unit equal to one hectare of land producing the world average yield of the relevant crop. It assumes the land being converted has typical rather than local productivity, so two regions with identical hectare areas can convert to different global hectares and still occupy the same physical ground. The measure is useful for comparing land demand across countries with very different yields, and misleading whenever a reader treats the converted figure as an area.

questions.explanation: A global hectare scales land by assumed productivity, so equal areas can convert differently. It is a demand comparison device and no longer a plain area once the yield assumption is built in.
questions.hint: Ask what the unit assumes about typical yield.

questions.topic: Which measure repays its embodied energy faster
questions.learningObjective: Explain why simple payback is often preferred to discounted payback

answer.exemplar: Simple payback divides the embodied energy by the annual net surplus and is preferred because it is transparent, needs no discount rate and shows the earliest year in which the investment is met. Discounted payback is more rigorous but reports a later, better-comparable figure because later surpluses count less, and for fast-repaying devices the difference between the two measures is small, which is why the simpler number is often quoted.

questions.explanation: Simple payback divides embodied energy by annual net surplus and reports the earliest repayment year without a discount rate. Discounted payback is more rigorous but always later, and for fast devices the gap is small.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a renewable source needs balancing
questions.learningObjective: Explain why firm capacity is needed on an intermittent network
questions.stem: A writing task asks us to explain why an intermittent feed needs a backup.

answer.exemplar: Wind output follows weather, not demand, so an annual mix of half wind can leave several consecutive days with little output while demand is at its winter peak. Firm capacity has to cover the worst net deficit period, not the annual total, because surplus wind hours that arrive earlier in the year do not reliably fall inside that window. Storage, interconnectors, dispatchable generation and demand response all contribute, and the adequacy assessment should test the longest and deepest shortfall rather than the average.

questions.explanation: An annual mix says nothing about whether supply matches demand in a particular week. Firm capacity must cover the deepest and longest shortfall, since earlier surplus need not arrive when it hits.
questions.hint: Think about the hours when the source produces nothing.

questions.topic: A stock and a flow of the same thing

answer.exemplar: Set up one catchment with a continuous level gauge on the reservoir, an inlet flow meter and an outlet withdrawal meter, and run the exercise across a planned drawdown. questions.topic: The rule that classifies a resource as renewable
questions.learningObjective: Explain the difficulty of applying the rate test to a national system
questions.stem: A product note asks how to judge renewable resources fairly.

answer.exemplar: The rate of renewal test asks whether a resource is regenerated at least as fast as it is taken. For a national system this is hard because extraction and regeneration cross administrative boundaries: water is abstracted in one catchment and returned in another, timber is felled in one region and consumed in another, and measured flows rarely match published regeneration estimates. The judgement then depends on bookkeeping choices about boundaries that the physical test alone cannot settle.

questions.explanation: The test compares regeneration with extraction on a system whose inputs and outputs cross boundaries. That boundary problem is why two jurisdictions can judge the same resource differently.
questions.hint: Ask whether the system boundary matches the resource.

answer.exemplar: Take the two inventories, list every stage each one includes, and mark the differences on a common stage list. answer.exemplar: One study may express land in physical hectares and the other in global hectares, which divides area by a yield assumption, so the same 5000 hectares can appear as 3500 global hectares where yields are above average and as 7000 where they are below. A reader should always check the unit and the boundary before treating a difference as a disagreement about the project.

questions.stem: An experiment ticket asks for a trial comparing payback measures side by side.

answer.exemplar: Select a set of projects that differ in asset life, in the timing of their cash flows and in scale, then compute a simple payback, a discounted payback and a levelised cost for each using one stated discount rate and one stated boundary. questions.topic: Which measure repays its embodied energy faster
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limits of a levelised cost for decision making
questions.stem: A note asks us to describe what a per-unit-energy cost leaves out.

answer.exemplar: A levelised cost per unit of energy lets two very different technologies be compared on one scale, which no other single figure allows. It should not stand alone, because it averages the whole life of the asset into one number: it says nothing about the timing of cash flows, the value of early delivery, the risks carried by the party building the asset, or the costs the boundary excluded. Two projects with the same levelised cost can leave the buyer in very different positions.

questions.explanation: Levelised cost compresses a whole asset life into one comparable number, which is its strength and its weakness. It hides timing, risk allocation and excluded costs.
questions.hint: Ask what the single number cannot show.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a renewable source needs balancing
questions.learningObjective: Describe two ways of providing balancing capacity
questions.stem: A documentation request asks why balancing matters for an intermittent feed.

answer.exemplar: An intermittent source produces when the weather allows, not when demand appears, so the system always carries a gap between what is generated and what is needed. Storage closes part of that gap by shifting energy in time, either as a battery or as water held above a turbine. Interconnection closes it by importing from a region whose weather is currently different, and dispatchable plant or demand response closes it by producing or reducing consumption on demand. The sizing rule is the worst net gap, not the annual total.

questions.explanation: Intermittency creates a gap between generation and demand in specific hours. Balancing closes it by shifting energy in time, moving it across a network, or changing supply on demand, and is sized on the worst gap.
questions.hint: Think about the hours when the source produces nothing.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why renewability is a rate question rather than a material property
questions.stem: A policy note asks how renewable status gets assigned to a resource.

answer.exemplar: A resource is renewable when the natural process that produces it can replace what is taken at least as fast as it is removed. The test is about rates rather than materials, because the same material can be renewable or not depending on how it is managed: fast-growing plantations are renewable while old-growth woodland is not, and a fishery is renewable only while the stock is left at a level the population can replace. Material type alone therefore cannot settle the question, and the rate test must be applied to each case.

questions.explanation: Renewability is a rate comparison, so the same material can qualify in one use and fail in another. Treating it as a property of the material rather than of the rate of use misclassifies both.
questions.hint: Ask how fast it returns, not what it is made of.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: What a reserve-to-production ratio does not say
questions.learningObjective: Compute a reserve-to-production ratio for a field
questions.stem: Ticket DATA-44 gives a lithium field with an estimated reserve of 12 million tonnes and extraction of 1.5 million tonnes a year. Give the reserve-to-production ratio in years.
questions.explanation: The ratio is 12 million tonnes of reserve divided by 1.5 million tonnes a year, which is 8 years of supply at current rates. It says nothing about the price needed to keep extraction at that pace.
questions.hint: Reserve tonnes divided by tonnes per year.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Why a renewable source needs balancing
questions.learningObjective: Test whether an annual target and an hourly promise can both hold
questions.stem: Our reliability guild is comparing a target of 90 percent annual renewable supply with a promise of no load shedding in any hour of the winter peak. What should the note conclude?

options.text: The two targets are identical, because an annual renewable share of 90 percent guarantees no shed hour
options.misconception: assumes an annual share guarantees hourly adequacy

options.text: The annual target is the binding one, because hourly adequacy follows from the yearly figure
options.misconception: assumes adequacy follows automatically from the annual share

options.text: Neither target can be assessed, because no system records hourly supply alongside annual shares
options.misconception: assumes hourly data never exists

options.text: The two targets can conflict, because 90 percent annually can still leave a deficit at the peak

questions.explanation: Step one converts the 90 percent annual figure into what it can deliver in the worst evening hour. Step two applies the no-shedding promise to that hour, and the two do not automatically agree.
questions.hint: Test the worst hour, not the yearly average.
